value.overview: The Lesser Swallow-tailed Swift (Panyptila cayennensis), also called the Cayenne Swift, is a small tropical swift with very narrow wings and a long, deeply forked tail. Its glossy dark plumage contrasts with a white throat, upper breast, and small white patches near the rump. It spends most of its life in flight, catching insects above forest, rivers, clearings, farms, and towns. The species is generally associated with warm, humid lowland environments.
value.classification: The Lesser Swallow-tailed Swift belongs to the swift family Apodidae and the order Apodiformes. It is one of two species in the genus Panyptila.
value.identification: This swift is about 13 cm long and has a slender, streamlined shape. Adults are mainly glossy black or blue-black, with a white throat and upper breast forming a narrow collar around the rear of the neck. Small white patches occur on the sides of the rump, and fresh wing feathers may show pale edges. The long, narrow wings and deeply forked tail are distinctive, although the tail is often held closed and appears as a single pointed extension.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southern Mexico through Central America and across much of northern and central South America, including Trinidad. It uses humid lowland evergreen forest, forest edges, secondary woodland, plantations, cultivated areas, broad rivers, lakes, clearings, and settled landscapes. In Costa Rica it is a resident of the lowlands rather than a seasonal visitor. It occurs on the Caribbean side in valleys and foothills to about 800 m, and on the Pacific side from the Parrita region southward, reaching at least about 1,000 m in parts of the General, Térraba, and Coto Brus valleys.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident throughout its range, including Costa Rica. Individuals may make local movements in response to weather, food, or breeding conditions, but it is not considered a regular long-distance migrant in Costa Rica.
value.breeding: The Lesser Swallow-tailed Swift builds an unusual tubular or sleeve-shaped nest from soft plant fibers, seed fluff, feathers, and other light materials held together with saliva. The nest may be attached beneath a branch or tree trunk and can also be placed on a building or other human-made structure. An internal shelf supports the eggs and young. Two or three white eggs are laid. In Costa Rica, breeding has been reported mainly from January through June.
value.dietFeeding: It feeds mainly on flying insects captured in the air. The swift usually forages over forest canopy, edges, clearings, pastures, cropland, rivers, and other open areas. Its long, narrow wings allow fast, agile flight, and it may hunt alone, in pairs, or in loose groups with other small swifts. Like other swifts, it obtains most food while airborne and rarely uses the ground for feeding.
value.behavior: The Lesser Swallow-tailed Swift is highly aerial and spends most of the day flying. Its flight is rapid and fluttering, with frequent changes in direction as it pursues insects. It may fly low over the canopy or high above open country, lakes, and rivers. Pairs are often seen together, and the species can associate loosely with other swifts. Nest sites may also serve as nighttime roosts for adults.

conservation.populationTrend: A reliable global population estimate and clearly documented population trend are not available.
